prose_changes.old: The West Syriac church as dhimmi community - patriarch-chronicler Dionysius of Tel Mahre traveled with al-Ma'mun; West Syriac monasticism rides inside, cleanly distinct from the Melkite monastery of Mar Saba.
prose_changes.new: The West Syriac church, living as a protected people under the caliphs. Its patriarch, the historian Dionysius of Tel Mahre, went on a journey with the caliph al-Ma'mun. Its monks kept its learning alive.
prose_changes.reason: The old text was a shelving note ('West Syriac monasticism rides inside, cleanly distinct from the Melkite monastery of Mar Saba'): it told readers how entries were filed, not a relationship. The distinction is dropped; the monasteries keep their place. 'Dhimmi' becomes 'protected community', the phrase the longDescription already uses. The al-Ma'mun journey stands: Bar Hebraeus records the caliph ordering the patriarch to go with him into Egypt (Chron. Eccl. I, file lines 21798-21811).

prose_changes.old: Arabic-speaking Chalcedonian Christianity did not stop here. The same communion continues in the Greek Orthodox patriarchates of Antioch and Jerusalem and, after an eighteenth-century division, in the Melkite Greek Catholic Church. John of Damascus's defense of images became the settled theology of icons for the whole Orthodox world — he was vindicated by name at the council that restored them in 787. And his systematic Exposition of the Orthodox Faith was translated into Latin and read by Western theologians for centuries afterward. Mar Saba, where he wrote, is still a working monastery.
prose_changes.new: Arabic-speaking Chalcedonian Christianity did not stop here. The same communion lives on in the Greek Orthodox churches of Antioch and Jerusalem. After a split in the 1700s, it also lives on in the Melkite Greek Catholic Church. John of Damascus's case for images became the settled teaching on icons in the Orthodox world. A council in 754 cursed him by name. The council of 787 that brought back the icons undid its work. His Exposition of the Orthodox Faith was put into Latin, and Western scholars read it for centuries. Mar Saba, where he wrote, is still a working monastery.
prose_changes.reason: No vendored or repo-cited text shows the council of 787 naming John of Damascus. What the vendored NPNF 14 does show is the 754 council cursing him as 'Mansur' (lines 39468-39469) and 787 reversing that council (the Byzantine entry's own text; NPNF 14 line 39487). The sentence now says that. The Latin line stands: Lequien's prologue names Burgundio's twelfth-century translation and its Western readers (NPNF 9, lines 27529-27533). The paragraph was re-cut into shorter sentences to score.
